CAMP COlINSEEOMtS 


Should bp 

-Camp Counselors ” 


Mary L. North way, 

Institute of Child Study, University of 7 oronto 


The modern camp counselor appar¬ 
ently should be a mixture of Superman 
and an archangel. According to pre¬ 
valent discussion, it is suggested he be 
trained at the graduate level in sociol¬ 
ogy, education, psychology, group work 
and numerous other subjects. In addi¬ 
tion to such training, he is expected to 
possess personality characteristics of 
intelligence, interest, honesty, tact, 
perseverance, diligence, tolerance, sym¬ 
pathy and, for good measure, a fine 
sense of humour. In time, perhaps, the 
human species will evolve such crea¬ 
tures; meanwhile, camp directors who 
wish any staff must fill the positions 
with ordinary human beings and ac¬ 
cept the varieties of virtues and frailties 
inherent in them. 

As long as we have to use human 
beings for our counselors, we will ex¬ 
pect to find both variety of training 
and variation of personality. But 
among the many possible assets the 
camp counselor may have, it seems 
that he must have two: ability to 
camp and ability to counsel. 

To camp means to live simply in the 
outdoors and to enjoy it. For many city 
dwellers this is not easy. One has to 
be clever to live simply. And one has 
to know, understand and love the out¬ 
door world to be comfortable in it. 


The counselor should therefore possess 
the skills for outdoor living which his 
particular camp situation requires. 
Camps themselves vary from the sum¬ 
mer hotel to the barracks, from central¬ 
ized regimentation to decentralized 
primitive living, from the school to the 
holiday, from the expensive to the 
free; some being situated in the lake 
country, others in the mountains or 
fields. One is reminded of the four- 
year-old who, seeing a St. Bernard, 
asked his mother; “What’s that?” 
“That’s a dog, dear; you know what 
a dog is.” “Yes”, he replied, “but some 
dogs look like dogs.” So some camps 
look like camps, but within the species 
there is as much variety to be found as 
amongst different breeds of dogs. 

It is difficult, therefore, to say just 
what skills the camp counselor must 
possess, other than that he needs those 
which arc appropriate to the type of 
camp. If he goes to a camp in the lake 
country, he should be able to manage 
boats, to feel secure in and on the 
water, to build fires, pitch tents, cook 
meals, foresee weather changes, etc. 
He should feel comfortable and know 
how to help his campers live comfort- 
ablv in the out-of-doors life of his 
camp. Camping skills are important, 
not as ends, but means to satisfy out¬ 
door living. 


Toronto, Canada, December, 1949 


/ 


As well as skills for outdoor living, 
he should be interested in the outdoor 
world. This does not mean he should 
be a “nature study expert'’, but rather, 
that he should be curious about the 
natural world. He need not send his 
campers to gather ten different plants 
and know their names, but he should 
feel the delight, which is contagious, in 
seeing plants grow, in watching the 
changing colour of the countryside, in 
appreciating the intricacies of tree 
growth and decay, in making effort to 
improve the natural resources of the 
camp site, in understanding the wider 
implications of conservation. He should 
know the value of time spent in doing 
nothing but watching. There are such 
good things to watch in the outdoors— 
waves breaking on beaches, stars 
gradually appearing in their constella¬ 
tions, northern lights, a sandpiper by 
the shore, skylines and the great white 
clouds on a blue summer day. There 
arc good things, too, to hear—the loon’s 
cry, a whippoorwill, the wind in the 
tops of the pine trees, the very strange 
silence of a still night. 

So often at camp there is no time 
left to stop and smell wood smoke or 
touch the softness of sphagnum or a 
clover patch on a hot summer day. 
“Program” is often so full there is no 
time left for living. Yet from enjoyment 
and observation of the outdoor world, 
interest is aroused in “why things hap¬ 
pen” and from such why’s, questions 
basic to science, philosophy and even 
religion arc aroused — questions fun¬ 
damental to the nature of the world 
and the human being’s place in it. The 
first quality, then, a counselor must 
have is to be able to camp—to know 
how to live in the outdoors and to be 
interested in the natural world. 

The second quality a counselor 
should have is the ability to counsel, to 
guide children’s development subtly yet 
surely. This depends primarily on the 


counselor being interested in children— 
more interested in children than in 
himself. It is fairly easy to thrust one’s 
own interests on children, more diffi¬ 
cult to become interested in theirs. For 
children’s interests are definitely “child¬ 
ish”. And many counselors, because 
of their own insecurities, feel it is 
slightly undignified to be concerned 
with the trivial activities youngsters 
enjoy. 

A college undergraduate at camp 
may find himself in charge of a group 
of five-year-olds. Filled with his own 
enthusiasms, he resolves to get these 
guys toughened up into athletes and 
turned into miniature replicas of him¬ 
self. So he herds them down to boat 
practice, boxing, or takes them on en¬ 
durance hikes. Through the use of 
badges, prizes, marks or the persuasion 
of his own dynamic personality, he 
inculcates “interests”, but they are his 
interests. 

It is a much more difficult task to 
be interested in the interests of his 
campers. In late adolescence one seems 
to forget what it was like to be a child. 
Later, one again remembers. So if the 
counselor cannot recall what it felt like 
at five to jump into fresh hay in a 
nearby farm field, or build a sand castle 
with a moat around it, or swing from 
trees, his best policy is to sit back and 
watch and listen. It is very difficult to 
recall the thrill of fishing for shiners 
or wading up a stream to see where it 
goes, or putting on a play that has 
seven acts in five minutes and no con¬ 
clusion. But these may be of vital 
importance to the young child. The 
counselor may say: “If we just let 
those youngsters play around at these 
things, they aren’t learning anything.” 
Aren’t they? Perhaps they are learning 
to enjoy life and to discover the possi¬ 
bilities of expressing interest in happy, 
constructive activity. Indeed, it is a 
travesty of adult modem life, we are 


8 


Canadian Camping 


so busy with recreation we have no 
time for play. We take so long being 
educated, we never get around to living. 

If the counselor has forgotten what 
children like to do, he may also have 
forgotten what it feels like to be very 
young. To a child the camp dining 
room may feel terrifyingly large. Strange 
night sounds of owls and loons or thun¬ 
der may make him afraid; being away 
from home for the first time may cause 
loneliness to the extent that he is 
literally sick. Fears of some children arc 
extremely real. One of the strange be¬ 
liefs of our society is that it is wrong 
to be afraid. The counselor himself 
inculcated with this belief may ridicule 
children’s fears or even condemn them. 
The child thus learns not to rid himself 
of the fears but to repress them. If 
the counselor wants to be a counselor , 
he must help the child accept the feel¬ 
ing of being afraid as something every¬ 
one experiences and help him under¬ 
stand it. For example, the loon that 
made the terrifying sounds at night 
may be observed on the sunlit blue lake 
the next day, so the camper gets to 
know and be interested in him. It is, 
of course, essential that no needless 
fears be engendered in the youngster. 
He need not be forced to swim in deep 
water right away; he may enjoy wading 
around the beach and playing with toy 
boats. Supernatural fears from spooky 
stories and myths about malicious 
ghosts have no place in the young 
camper’s life, nor have real fears of 
night raids, hazing, etc. There are 
enough things to be afraid of in the 
civilized, atomic world, that there is no 
need to produce artificial terrors. 

Finally, if the counselor is really 
concerned wth the campers’ develop¬ 
ment, he must remember that young 
children require a great deal of time and 
a great deal of guidance in dealing with 


the “daily round and common task”. 
The college student may think it a little 
dull and undignified to supervise the 
camper washing his hands and face 
(and neck occasionally), to plan time 
for him to go to the toilet, to help him 
be interested in keeping his cabin 
reasonably tidy, eating his meals quietly 
and adequately, remembering that but¬ 
tons have to be sewn on and shorts 
patched, sending clothes to the laundry; 
these are all part of the routines of 
living which the camper is not ready 
to assume all by himself, but which he 
is ready to learn. Too often camp pro¬ 
grams are so extremely busy that little 
time is allotted for these daily tasks, 
but as soon as these are not taken care 
of, the camper’s life and the camp’s 
life become a drastic muddle. To coun¬ 
sel wisely must include helping the 
youngster to develop skill and interest 
in necessary routines and to take time 
and thought to work out plans by which 
this can be achieved. To counsel, then, 
means that the life, interests and feel¬ 
ings of youngsters are the counselor’s 
primary concern, for only with an 
understanding of these can his guidance 
be developed effectively. 

A camp counselor should be a camf) 
counselor. He should have “a sense of 
at-homeness in the natural world and 
the arts of outdoor living”, *and he 
should be able to counsel:—guide de¬ 
velopment by understanding the child’s 
level of maturity, interest and skill. 
With these qualities he will perhaps not 
be a Superman, but he will be an in¬ 
valuable asset to any camp staff and a 
great surprise and satisfaction to 
himself. 


*—Dimock, H.— Administration of the 
Modern Camp. Association Press, New 
York; G. R. Welch Company, Toronto. 


Toronto , Canada , December , 1949

HEALTH 


and Safety Standards 

J. H. Ebbs, M.D., M.R.C.P. (Lond.), F.R.C.P. (C). 


The increase in the number of camps 
and the large number of children who 
now enjoy the pleasures and advan¬ 
tages of camp life, make it essential that 
standards be adopted. Any organization 
which accepts children under its care, 
must consider its responsibilities, and 
practice accepted methods for health 
and safety. Government regulations 
direct the type of sanitary arrangements 
in summer camps. The fundamentals 
of health and safety are of primary con¬ 
cern to every camp director. Health 
and safety practices are the responsi¬ 
bility of the camp staff and may vary 
in each camp. The Committee for 
Health and Safety of the Canadian 
Camping Association will keep camp 
leaders informed about the standards 
which are being formulated in the vari¬ 
ous sections of Canada. 

In presenting the minimum Stand¬ 
ards of the Ontario Camping Associa-* 
tion (adopted in 1949), it should be 
pointed out that these are minimum 
standards, which every camp should 
be able to meet. From time to time 
these standards will be reviewed and 
it is hoped they will be raised to ap¬ 
proach desirable standards. 

The Committee of Standards is under 
the Chairmanship of Mr. John Hoyle. 


Minimum Standards for Organized 
Camps in Ontario as recommended by 
The Ontario Camping Association. 

Definition : An organized camp is one 
which accommodates more than 
twelve campers for more than one 
week. 

HEALTH AND SAFETY 

1. A Licence must be obtained from 
the Provincial Department of 
Health approving all sanitary 
arrangements. 

2. Drinking water must be approved 
by the Provincial Department of 
Health before camp opens. 

3. All milk must be pasteurized. 

4. A hot bath, shower or similar 
facilities must be provided weekly 
in camps of more than two weeks’ 
duration. 

5. Every camp must have the services 
of a qualified medical doctor, who 
is available for consultation on 
matters of healh and sanitation. 
If not resident, arrangements for 
him to be on call must be made 
before the opening of camp. 

6. Every camp must have a person, 
in residence, who is trained in first 
aid. 

7. There must be a resident nurse in 
camps of more than two weeks’ 
duration and with more than thirty 
children. 


10 Canadian Camping 


8. Every camper, and all members of 
the staff, must have a health ex¬ 
examination by a medical doctor 
within two weeks of attending 
camp. 

9. A rest period of not less than one 
hour daily must be provided for 
both stalT and campers. 

LEADERSHIP 

1. All prospective staff members must 
be investigated thoroughly by the 
sponsoring body with reference to 
their character, emotional stability 
and physical fitness. 

2. Where an applicant for a staff 
position has been associated with 
another camp or organization, the 
camp must contact the director of 
the previous camp or organization 
in regard to (1) above. 

3. A counselor (or full staff member) 
must not be less than seventeen 
years of age. 

4. A r amp must not have less than 
one cabin or group counselor (a) 
for every six campers who are 
under ten years of age, and (b) 
one such counselor for every eight 
campers who arc between ten and 
seventeen years of age. (In the 
case of Boy Scouts, the trained 
patrol leader may be considered as 
meeting the requirements under 
section “b” and in the case of Girl 
Guides by Senior Guides of Six¬ 
teen) . 

5. In the absence of the camp direc¬ 
tor from camp, his authority must 
be delegated specifically to some 
other qualified person. 

6. In camps of more than two weeks’ 
duration all staff members mest 
have an adequate period each 
week entirely free from camp re¬ 
sponsibility. (A minimum of one 
half of a working day per week is 
suggested.) 


WATERFRONT 

1. The swimming and diving area 
must be investigated and approved. 

2. All equipment such as docks, div¬ 
ing boards, canoes, boats, etc., must 
be inspected yearly and approved 
for safety. 

3. All waterfront and water-craft ac¬ 
tivity must be under the super¬ 
vision of a person fully qualified 
in life saving and waterfront 
safety. 

4. There must be a thorough life¬ 
guard system in operation while 
swimmers are in the water at a 
minimum ratio of one life-guard 
to every ten persons swimming. 
While on such duty a life-guard 
must have no other duty or dis¬ 
traction. 

5. Proper safety provision must be 
made for staff, cooks, handymen, 
and all other employees, and visi¬ 
tors, while swimming or in water¬ 
craft. Under no circumstances 
shall anybody swim alone. 

6. Individual swimming tests must be 
tried as soon after arrival at camp 
as possible and before swimming is 
allowed in other than shallow 
water. 

7. No person must be allowed alone 
in any water-craft in water beyond 
his depth before he has passed the 
required tests for that particular 
type of water-craft. 

8. Rules regarding swimming and 
diving on out-trips must be stated 
clearly and enforced strictly. 

9. Boats and canoes other than life 
saving patrol boats must not be al¬ 
lowed in the swimming area. 

10. Swimmers must not be allowed 
to hang on to, or interfere in any 
way, with the life saving patrol 
boats. 


Toronto , Canada, December , 1949 


II 


11. No person must be allowed to 
swim any considerable distance 
(as determined by the person in 
charge of the waterfront) outside 
the swimming area without being 
accompanied by a boat carrying 
two persons, one of whom must be 
a qualified life-saver. Such a boat 
must carry adequate life-saving 
apparatus. 


l'IRE PROTECTION 

Every care shall be taken in light¬ 
ing and extinguishing camp and 
hike fires. Every camp must be 
provided with filled fire buckets or 
their equivalent. Sand buckets 
must be provided if oil is used.

A MESSAGE 


from Our President-elect 


Meeting with the Camping Club of 
Great Britain and hearing of the limited 
space for camping there, gave me a 
deeper realization of our great resources 
in Canada, the riches we possess and 
the tremendous significance of this heri¬ 
tage. Possession brings responsibility, 
which together we can share. We stand 
expectantly on the threshold of great 
developments in camping. 

As we look forward to the Christmas 
season, I recall my last Christmas, rich 
in experience and fellowship, and spent 
far away in England. On returning 
home, after eight months abroad, one 
of the joys I anticipated was the renew¬ 
ing of my contacts with camping friends 
across Canada. 


As your newly-elected President, and 
on behalf of the new officers and board 
of your Canadian Camping Association, 
may I greet our members from coast to 
coast. We assure you it is our desire 
and purpose to serve you to the best of 
our ability. 

May we give you at this time our 
National Office address: 2035 Coursol 
Street, Montreal, P.Q. There you can 
reach us and your requests and sug¬ 
gestions will receive every consideration. 

Let us all go forward together into 
the New Year with the determination 
that we will make 1950 a very special 
year of progress in our Canadian Camp¬ 
ing Association. 

—ANNE I. VAIL 



12 


Canadian Camping 


I V EXPERIMENT 


la HANDICRAFTS 


Gisela Commanda, A.R.C.A. 


The Ontario Department of Educa¬ 
tion is carrying out an interesting ex¬ 
periment at Camp Belwood, near Fer¬ 
gus, in counselor-training and last sum¬ 
mer one hundred and sixty young 
people were given a three weeks’ inten¬ 
sive course to fit them to be counselors 
in non-profit camps. At the request of 
Mr. C. T. Sharpe, Supervisor of Camp¬ 
ing for the Department of Education 
in the province of Ontario, the writer 
was asked to give instruction in crafts 
which would involve inexpensive 
materials and only a few tools. 

After completing an art course and 
teaching in England, I came to Canada, 
where I married an Ojibway Indian 
and spent many months in the 
Nippissing Reserve. While living 
among the Indians, I always interested 
myself deeply in their customs and most 
particularly in their crafts and designs. 
Therefore, it seemed natural and im¬ 
portant for me to choose Indian Craft 
as a basis for this course in handicraft. 
This involved making use of natural 
Canadian materials, many of which can 
be gathered around the camp, instead 
of choosing such things as shell craft, 
felt flowers, etc., which must be pur¬ 
chased from commercial firms. 

There was no expense attached to 
the excellent Indian craft work done in 
Canada before the coming of the white 
man. There was only the time and skill 
involved in collecting and preparing 
the material. The forest still offers to¬ 
day splendid natural materials and since 
most camps are situated in forest sur¬ 


roundings, it seems logical to study the 
use the Indians made of natural mater¬ 
ials; also their colours, designs, symbols 
and folk lore. A growing knowledge of 
these things will result in a deepened 
interest in the whole subject. 

Birch bark is wonderful material, 
but since it was not available at Camp 
Belwood, we secured two sacks of it and 
one of fresh cedar wood for carving. 
An Indian type of birch bark canoe, 
about a foot long, was made as a 
sample. The seats and paddles were of 
carved cedar and the seams were 
caulked with Le Page’s glue. These 
little models would delight the heart of 
any small boy, who would probably take 
them to the lake and float them. Many 
other things were made out of the bark, 
including miniature baskets with 
handles, painted with Indian symbols. 
The students discovered for themselves 
that colourless nail polish preserves 
their water colour designs on the bark 
when it is in the water. They also in¬ 
vented attractive painted birch bark 
bracelets. 

The outside silver layer of the bark 
is useless for craft work, but can be 
saved to make a pleasant flare and smell 
in the camp fire at night. The inner¬ 
most bark is pale gold and a beautiful 
surface for water colour paintings. The 
in-between brown layers can be rubbed 
to a polish and are also suitable for 
painting. Sometimes the campers sat 
under the trees, peeling the bark into 
layers. Some of them took away the 
thin paper-weight layers on which to 


Toronto, Canada, December, 1949 


13 


write letters. In the painting class, we 
sang camp songs such as “Land of the 
Silver Birch”. This was followed by 
attemps to illustrate it, without pencils, 
in direct brush work. Later, the stu¬ 
dents, having caught on to the idea, 
went off and painted sunsets on the 
bark, in their free time. 

Another craft was building miniature 
log cabins out of half-inch twigs gath¬ 
ered from under trees, notching them 
at the corners with a jack knifs and 
sticking each layer with glue. These 
had door and window openings with 
frames ol cedar. Various kinds of cones 
can be made into Christmas decora¬ 
tions, place cards, etc. 

I had designed toy animals, circus 
horses, clowns, Harlequins and Colum¬ 
bines, which we cut out of cardboard 
and stuck into cardboard stands, rang¬ 
ing from five to twelve inches in height. 
We also had Indian figures with sets of 
traditional costumes to fit them. 

Marionettes intrigued the campers. 
We made large, flat cardboard, jointed 
marionettes, one and a half feet high. 
They were dressed in materials and 
adorned like the circus horses and 
theatre folk, with wool work, fancy 
braid sewn on, gold paper and Christ¬ 
mas gummed stars. Wigs were made of 
wool or unravelled potato sacks for less 
expensive ones. Corrugated store boxes 
form excellent stages, with the front cut 
out for the proscenium opening. The 
front was decorated, curtains added, 
and the tiny marionettes of jointed 
cardboard were the players. 

To supplement the practical work 
there were lecture periods for theory. 
For the first lecture, I wore my buck¬ 
skin costume and showed the campers 
Indian figures dressed in traditional 
outfits, explaining also how they were 
made. I showed them a whole eagle 
skin and told of how the Indian head¬ 


dress developed from the natural ar¬ 
rangement of the feathers on the upper 
wings. There were also samples of In¬ 
dian handwork, such as moccasins and 
buckskins, to examine. In another lec¬ 
ture we took histories and incidents ol 
Harlequin and Columbine, Punch and 
Judy, marionettes, puppets, clowns, 
etc., and that charming host of charac¬ 
ters, real and fictitious, used so often by 
craftsmen and artists. The last lecture 
was on the theory of handicraft 
teaching. 

Anyone intend'ng to teach crafts in 
a non-profit camp should have a few 
cartons in which to collect suitable scrap 
material throughout the year, such as 
pieces of cloth, Christmas wrappings, 
stars, ribbons, tinsel, etc. Friends can 
often help fill the boxes for use the 
following summer in camp. Many 
people are so accustomed to using only 
correct materials with all the tools, that 
they fail to see the exciting possibilities 
of creating simple things out of inex¬ 
pensive “odds and ends”. 



14 


Canadian Camping 


Ontario Honours 


Camp Director 


The Honourable Dana Porter, At¬ 
torney-General and Minister or Educa¬ 
tion, recently presented to Mr. A. L. 
Cochrane (of Toronto), Director of 
Camp Tcmagami, a handsome metal 
plaque mounted on a wood background. 
This was the government’s tribute to 
his services to Ontario’s youth through 
fifty years as director of his well-known 
camp. 



Mr. Cochrane is now in his eightieth 
year, and still able to give a most re¬ 
markable account of himself in the 
vigorous physical activities associated 
with camping. 

One of the annual events most antici¬ 
pated by Camp Temagami’s campers 
and staff is the Chief’s (“A.L.’s”) stunt 
of permitting himself to be tossed from 


the dock into the lake, sewn up in a 
sack along with a ten pound stone, and 
with his hands and feet tied!! This year, 
as in all others, he was back to the sur¬ 
face and on the dock in a matter of less 
than one minute. 

Latin phrase embodied in the tablet 
is at once a tribute both to Mr. Coch¬ 
rane personally, and to his objectives 
and achievements with boys — Ad 
Unguem Factus Homo —“A man to his 
fingertips”, or “Every inch a man”. 

The Canadian Camping Association 
is extremely proud of its Honorary 
President. In the words of our new 
President, Ann Vail: “He has been a 
tower of strength to the Camping Asso¬ 
ciation and we all appreciate his sup¬ 
port. He has never failed us with that”. 



’ Toronto } Canada, December, 1949 


15 



















The Editor Comments 


In this issue wc are happy to give 
you a message from Anne Vail, our new 
Prcsicbnt, elected unanimously at the 
Annual Meeting of the Canadian 
Camping Association held in Ottawa, 
November 11th- 13 th. 

Driving to Ottawa on November 
11th, wc listened with sobering memo¬ 
ries to the broadcast of the impressive 
Armistice Day service, in front of the 
Cenotaph in our Capital. We remem¬ 
bered the high hopes with which a war- 
weary world entered hopefully into the 
first Armistice service of 1919. 

Between sessions of the board meet¬ 
ings, wc took time to visit the exquisite 
Memorial Chapel of the Parliament 
Buildings. There the memorable words 
of our soldier-poet, John McCrac, are 
engraved in white marble and once 
again their challenge “to us in our 
time”, was clear and poignant. 

“To you from failing hands 
Wc throw the torch; 

Be yours to hold it high.” 

From the top of the Peace Tower, wc 
meditated on those words and realized 
it is only to the Youth of our country 
today that wc can repay the terrific 


debt we owe to the Canadian youth of 
two world wars. Gazing east, west, 
north and south, from that slender 
tower which dominates Capitol Hill, 
there is a wide vista of city streets, 
curving rivers, fields, woods and far 
hills, and beyond those blue horizons lie 
the wide stretches of our vast land. 
There in the ten provinces, reaching 
the Atlantic and Pacific, yes, even the 
far Arctic—there is growing up the 
new gencrat ; on of boys and girls to 
whom our Canadian Camping Associa¬ 
tion must pay a debt and toward which 
wc must work and plan and dream. We 
returned to the deliberations of the 
board meetings with a deepened sense 
of the significance of our responsibility. 

The newly-elected executive and 
board members devoted much time to 
a study of definite and desirable goals to 
which the Association should move 
forward in 1950. These goals, which 
will be set forth in the next issue of 
this magazine, were accepted as a defi¬ 
nite commitment and involve a stan¬ 
dard of better and more effective ser¬ 
vice to the whole Camping movement 
in Canada. Thus shall the C.C.A. 
strive in the New Year, to discharge 
part of its debt to Youth.

Of General interest 

A meeting of the board of the Cana¬ 
dian Camping Association was held at 
the Chateau Laurier in Ottawa, Nov. 
11 - 13, at which time an interim execu¬ 
tive was elected, to serve until the 
Annual Meeting in February (as 
authorized by the constitution). 

The newly-elected executive is as 
follows: 

Anne Vail President Montreal 

Irwin Haladner 1st Vice-Pres. Toronto 
W. E. (Ted) Yard 2nd Vice-Pres. Toronto 
(Nominated by the B.C. and Sask. Assoc’ns) 
Agnes Mutchler Secretary Montreal 
Ernest Freedman Treasurer Montreal 

Business of great importance was 
given serious consideration at each ses¬ 
sion, and some very definite and signifi¬ 
cant objectives were unanimously 
agreed upon as goals for 1950. These 
will be presented in the next issue of 
Canadian Camping.

The Camping Club of Great Britain 
and Ireland publishes a most interesting 
little magazine, “Camping and Outdoor 
Life”. Annual subscription 6s. 6d. (7 
issues). Orders may be sent to Rolls 
House Publishing Co. Ltd., 2 Breams 
Bids., London E.C.4, England. There 
is a memberhsip of over 10,000, and the

Council of fifteen elected members. The 
Patron is H.M. the King.

son, St. Louis, Mo., February 15 - 18. 
1950. 

There will be top speakers, discussion 
groups, camping “know-how” and fine 
fellowship.

NOTES 

from the Provinces 

BRITISH COLUMBIA 

At the request of the Camping Sec¬ 
tion of the Vancouver Community 
Chest, the B.C. Camping Association 
conducted a survey on the probable 
lack of girls’ camps. We have a large 
number of boys’ camps, i.e., Y.M.C.A., 
Boys’ Club, etc., with a much smaller 
number of camps for girls only. The 
matter was approached, firstly, upon 
the needs for camping facilities for girls; 
secondly, upon what camps arc avail¬ 
able for girls. The findings of the com¬ 
mittee have not yet been brought to 
the Association. 

The B.C. Camping Association has 
been invited to take part in the Can¬ 
adian Association for Health, Physical 
Education and Recreation national 
convention, to be held in Vancouver 
next June. A committee is busy working 
out a program that will include a sea 
trip visit to several camps. 

ONTARIO 

AN EXPERIMENT IN 
ALL-SUMMER TRAINING 

During the camp season of 1949, the 
Ontario Council Girl Guides Associa¬ 
tion operated a Leadership Training 
Camp. Five ten-day camps were held, 
and during each period three separate 
camps were operated. 

In the first group were Patrol Lead¬ 
ers, age 13 to 15, and their camp served 
as the model camp for the training of 
older leaders. These girls worked on 
their Pioneer badge, and did consider¬ 
able swimming and canoeing; they 
learned to take responsibility for their 
own patrols of five or six girls. 

In the second group were girls 16 to 
19, who were training to become camp 
staff. These girls worked at perfecting 


their own skills, and were also given 
training in leadership. 

In the third group were Guiders of 
over 21 years of age, who had had 
previous camp experience as staff. 
These were trained as Camp Directors, 
and given training in all aspects of 
Camp Administration, both in theory 
and practice. They spent some time in 
the Patrol Leader’s Camp both observ¬ 
ing and working with the girls, as well 
as doing practical and theoretical work 
with the trainer. 

The results of the summer were most 
satisfactory. There were about two 
hundred campers and twenty-three 
staff members during the season. The 
Ontario Council hopes to make the 
camp permanent. 

QUEBEC 

The Quebec Section seems to be off 
to a good start this autumn. Two 
meetings were held even before all the 
camps were tucked away at the end of 
the season. 

The October meeting was so well 
attended as to cause same slight mis¬ 
givings to the Social Convener, Ruby 
Smith, when she counted the house 
before serving the cakes and coffee. 

The program arranged by Roy Lock 
was different and stimulating. For the 
most part, youth took over and did a 
sound job. Short talks on swimming, 
canoe trips, religion in camp programs, 
counselor personality problems, peculiar 
camper behaviour and Nature experi¬ 
ences all related to experiences of the 
past summer, were handled with a nice 
mixture of seriousness and humour. 

NEW BRUNSWICK 

A year ago last Spring a New Bruns¬ 
wick branch of the Canadian Camping 
Association was organized. Through 
this agency a survey is being made of 
present Camping conditions in the pro¬ 
vince, and plans were developed for a 
Camp Leadership Course last Spring.

Book Reviews 


IT’S WISE TO SUPERVISE: com¬ 
piled and edited by Alan Klein and 
Irwin Haladncr; distributors, Ontario 
Camping Association, 236 Bloor St. 
W., Toronto; price .50. 

This practical little booklet has been 
prepared through the collaboration of 
two experienced Camp leaders, Alan 
Klein, Director of Camp Northland, 
and Assistant Professor of Social Work, 
University of Toronto, and Irwin 
Haladner, Director of Camp Wabi-Kon 
and past president of the Ontario 
Camping Association. 

Supervision in Camp is interpreted as 
a most essential part of the Director’s 
administrative job. Many practical 
suggestions are given for educating 
the Counselor to his unique opportunity 
in the Camp community—making him 
aware of the importance of his job 
through a scries of helpful pre-camp 
letters, cooperative staff meetings and 
understanding guidance. To attain the 
goal of happy team-work in Camp, it 
is “wise to’supervise”. This small book 
suggests methods, and emphasizes the 
fact that even experienced Directors 
have much to learn on the subject. 

ONE HUNDRED STORIES FOR 
BOYS: by Archer Wallace; Ryerson 
Press, Toronto; pp. 264; price $2.00. 

Camp directors are constantly on the 
look-out for “human interest” short 
stories which they can use in assembly 
or chapel talks. Averaging about five 
hundred words in length, these stories

are about historical characters, ranging 
from ancient times (Alexander the 
Great) to modern baseball heroes (Lou 
Gehrig). Also included are incidents 
from the lives of missionaries, scientists, 
writers, explorers, statesmen and others. 
The characters include Hans Christian 
Anderson, Edward Bok, Joseph Conrad, 
Thomas Edison, David Livingston, 
Fritz Kreisler, Louis Pasteur, Booker 
T. Washington and many others. 

Counselors will find the book of great 
value for use as illustrative material. 

GOLDEN NORTH: by Marie Me- 

Phcdran; MacMillan Co. of Canada, 

Ltd., Toronto; pp. 192; price, $2.50. 

This is a story that will appeal to all 
campers who know the adventure of a 
camping trip. They will envy the young 
lad, Ricky, who gets the chance to go 
with two prospectors into the wilder¬ 
ness of lakes and streams beyond The 
Pas, in northern Manitoba, in the quest 
for gold. 

They will gain much practical infor¬ 
mation about real camping out in the 
northern wilderness and will thrill to 
the excitement of staking a claim and 
finding a gold mine. Best of all, they 
will learn of the prospector’s deep, un¬ 
spoken love of the north, and will gain 
a new sense of wonder as they learn 
about Canada’s amazing Pre Cambrian 
Shield, which spreads from Hudson 
Bay almost to the Rockies, and hides in 
its great folds untold mineral wealth. 

Girl campers, too, will envy Ricky 
his adventures in the Golden North.

Canadian Camping 


THE LEFT HANDSHAKE, by Hilary 
St. George Saunders; Collins; ob¬ 
tainable from the Boy Scout Head¬ 
quarters, Northern Ontario Building, 
Toronto; price, $3.25. 

This is a stirring account of Scouting 
during the war. One would have to 
search far back in history to find a 
period when young men packed so 
much experience of living into six years. 
Oppression, disease, bereavement, tor¬ 
ture, starvation and death were the 
common lot, but Scouting stood the 
test, and its spirit provoked some of the 
finest deeds of courage in the annals 
of peace or war. It is right that the 
story of these grim years in the history 
of Scouting should be told, both as a 
record and as an inspiration for the 
future. The author has planned his 
book well, and his lively style is well 


suited to the telling of these tremendous 
adventures, where Scout membership 
in war became a most dangerous way 
of showing patriotism. 

The book starts dramatically with 
the story of a hero of the Dutch resis¬ 
tance who helped prevent the retreating 
Germans from blowing up a strategic 
bridge. Scouting, though banned in all 
the occupied countries, not only sur¬ 
vived, but helped inspire its members. 
In Poland secret schools sprang up, run 
by troop leaders for their Scouts. In 
the prisons Scouting flourished and 
saved the captives’ minds from sinking 
to the level of their weakened bodies. 
So the story carries on, giving many 
heroic episodes, until the clouds began 
to break and the work was carried on 
by teams of the Scout International 
Relief Service.

THE ST. NICHOLAS ANTHOL¬ 
OGY: Commager Henry Steele 

(Ed.). Random House, N.Y. Price, 
$6.00. (Obtainable in Canada from 
The T. Eaton Co. or The Robert 
Simpson Company). 

This is a collection of more than 
sixty stories and some of them arc 
quite tellable. They are mostly for 
boys, and have a leaning towards the 
sentimental (boys and girls arc more 
sentimental than we think) and arc 
dated in style (nineties), but could be 
easily modernized by the telling. There 
arc animal and sport stories, a few 
historical, and a collection of tales 
about boys and girls. Naturally the 
book has an American slant, but it 
does include a story about Grenfell, 
by Grenfell, also a good one on David 
Livingstone and another on the boy¬ 
hood of Charles Dickens. There are two 
or three stories which could be read 
aloud and chuckled at. It is a good 
book for your chief teller of tales, and 
will supply a quantity of fresh material 
for this summer.

CRY-O-RAP BAGS FOR 
CANOE TRIPS 

Packing food for camping trips 
always involves some problems. There 
arc some things which will not go into 
tins, and paper bags are unsatisfactory. 
For that reason, campers will welcome 
the new Cry-O-Rap bags. These arc 
specially designed plastic bags in a 
variety of sizes, intended for use in 
the frozen food industry. They are 
grand for keeping vegetables and fruits 
crisp and fresh. Bread will keep for 
eight days when properly scaled and 
will not become tainted with odours 
from other foods such as onions, coffee, 
etc. The bags will last a long time if 
reasonable care is taken, and they can 
be rinsed out and used over and over 
again. They can be purchased in three 
sizes and arc quite inexpensive. Avail¬ 
able previously only from the Frozen 
Locker trade, they can now be pur¬ 
chased from the Lewis Craft Supplies 
Limited, 645 Yongc Street, Toronto 
2-B. 

FUN FOR A RAINY DAY- 
BIOGRAPHERS AND VICTIMS 
Set campers to work on biographies 
of each other. Have ready a stack of 
old magazines—the more, the merrier. 
Deal out to each a laundry shirt card¬ 
board or a piece of heavy paper. Pro¬ 
duce paste and as many pairs of scissors 
as possible. First comes a secret draw¬ 
ing of names, so no one knows who his 
biographer is to be. Next a scramble 
for magazines. Clip out baby pictures, 
headlines, cartoons, photographs, anec¬ 
dotes, ads—whatever will add to the 
hilarity and characterize the victim. 
Then stage an exhibit and let everyone 


Canadian Camping 






find himself. Present some foolish prize 
for the most uproariously clever 
biography. 

A FAVORITE RECIPE 
This simple dish is simply called 
“Campers’ Stew”. It is tasty, substan¬ 
tial and extremely easy to prepare. All 
that is required is a tin of pork and 
beans and a tin of beef hash or beef 
steak and onions. Heat the two together 
and serve either with the usual potatoes 
and vegetables on hand, or serve on 
toast.

Once there was a camper 

Who inscribed a Christmas note 
Addressed to “Dear Old Santa Claus”, 
And this is what she wrote: 

“You need not fill my stocking, 

Nor dock my Christmas tree: 

Among your wares, you haven’s got 
What most appeals to me. 

The “Super” thing I’m wishing for.— 
More than anything at all, 

Is word that I may go to camp 
Next year, from Spring till Fall.” 

—M.S.E. 

A ten-year-old camper rushed into 
the camp office. 

“Our cabin counselor’s being chased 
by a bull”, he said. 

“What can I do about it?”, said the 
Business Administrator. 

“Put a new roll of film in my 
camera!” 

There arc three kinds of people: 

Shirkers 

Jerkcrs 

Workers 

A child prodigy is one who merely 
comes up to his parents’ expectations.

A SIMPLE INEXPENSIVE DISHWASHING MACHINE 
ENDORSED BY MANY HEALTH AUTHORITIES 


THE WHIRLPOOL DISHWASHER 


SIMPLE INSTALLATION 
LOW IN COST 



Typical 3 Compartment Whirlpool Installation.

HIGH IN PERFORMANCE 
Once installed in a typical 3-compartment 
sink, as illustrated above, the Whirlpool way 
of washing dishes or glasses is simplicity 
itself. 


To install a Whirlpool Dish- 
washer no expensive 
changes are needed. If the 
washing compartment of 
your present sink measures 
approximately 19 inches 
wide, 24 inches front to 
back and 14 inches deep— 
or can be altered to these 
dimensions—that is all you 
require. You then stand 
the machine in place (it 
weighs only 55 pounds), 
plug the three-point elec¬ 
tric cord into the nearest 
wall plug, turn the switch 
and ihe Whirlpool is ready 
for work.

satisfaction by hospitals, restaurants, schools, industrial plants and
